solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Respond amiably to trick Hamlet?

blocks.note: to trick someone is to fool or deceive them, a phrasal verb of four plus two letters
Hamlet is a fine role for an actor; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: Someone is asked how to react gracefully when a prank is played on Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet looks like the prince or the play, but here he is a meaty acting role, which the question mark admits is just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept a remark or joke without offence is the idiom's meaning, which is responding with good humour.

clue.text: Try from Bath leaving sides to draw

indicators.note: when a word leaves its sides, its two edge letters are dropped and only the inside stays

blocks.note: the inner pair of letters of this word
to draw someone in is to entice or lure them

explanation.surface: A sporting try, perhaps in rugby, comes from the Bath side, whose players leave the touchlines to score a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath, the English spa city with a famous rugby club, makes 'Try' look like a rugby score; it is simply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, a try is an effort or go at something, exactly the sense of an attempt.

clue.text: As PM he is somehow last to acknowledge stress

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters arrive in an order still to be worked out
the last of a word is its final letter, so only the closing letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
final letter of this word

explanation.surface: A prime minister is somehow always the last person to admit to feeling under stress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stress' sits at the end looking like part of what the PM acknowledges; it is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress a point is to give it special weight or importance, the same verb in British spelling.

clue.text: Snacks sent up, like this hotel is able to

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top, so the order flips

blocks.note: so means in this way, as in 'do it so'
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
can means is able to

explanation.surface: A hotel boasts it can send snacks up to the rooms just like this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' reads like room service to the surface, but in a down clue it turns the string upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: These tortilla chips topped with cheese and salsa are a popular Mexican bar food, so they are one kind of snack.

clue.text: Watches, say, adding seconds

blocks.note: to say or remark is to observe, as in 'he observed that it was late'
S is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: Wristwatches, for example, gain a seconds hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watches, say' looks like wristwatches given as an example; in fact 'Watches' is a verb and 'say' gives a separate verb meaning to remark.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who watches a scene carefully looks at it attentively, which is the plain synonym sense here.

clue.text: Overturned soil packs empty ditches

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped over, so its letters run the other way
an emptied word has lost its contents, leaving only its outer shell of letters

blocks.note: mud is wet soil
first and last letters of this word

explanation.surface: Turned-over earth fills the drainage ditches that had been empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditches' looks like the trenches being filled, but it is a verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To ditch something is to get rid of or abandon it, the same as to throw it away.

clue.text: Ill-disposed to accept daughter is bad

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one word receives another inside it

blocks.note: averse means opposed or unwilling
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent unwilling to take their daughter back is behaving badly.
explanation.walkthrough: D, the genealogy abbreviation for daughter, slips in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse conditions or effects are harmful and unfavourable, which is a common sense of bad.

clue.text: Cast, well-organized, assembled quickly

blocks.note: cast as a past participle means tossed or hurled
a together person is calm and well organised

explanation.surface: A theatre cast, well drilled, was put together in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' reads as a group of actors, but it is a past participle. The irony is that the answer means the opposite of well organised.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hastily made or improvised with little planning is described by this phrase, so it fits a rushed assembly.

clue.text: University golf lessons with no clubs or visual aids

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so something is taken away from the word before it

blocks.note: Reading is an English town with a university
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet
lessons are classes
C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit

explanation.surface: A university offers golf lessons without clubs or visual aids such as videos.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs look like golf clubs but are the card suit, losing one letter from the front of the lessons word. Reading is a town west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles worn for close work help the eyes focus on print, so they are aids to vision.

clue.text: City borders of Toronto still in the wrong place

indicators.note: the borders of a region are its edges, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: EC is the postcode area of the City of London
first and last letters of the city name
a still is a photograph, a pic

explanation.surface: A city on the edge of Toronto is still somehow in the wrong spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City' is not Toronto: EC is the postcode for the City, London's financial district. 'Still' looks like an adverb but is a noun, a single photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: Medically, an ectopic pregnancy or organ is one located away from its normal position in the body.

clue.text: Large brewer run by Victor in an island state

indicators.note: being in something means being placed inside it

blocks.note: V is Victor in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Samoa is an island nation in the Pacific
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A big beer producer is managed by a man called Victor in an island country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brewer' suggests beer, but what is brewed here is tea. 'Run by' puts the run beside the rest, at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A samovar is a big Russian metal urn for heating water to make tea, so it is a large tea-making vessel.

clue.text: Conduct could be humbler from a dictator

indicators.note: someone dictating speaks words for another to write down, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: one who humbles or debases others could be called a demeaner

explanation.surface: A dictator's behaviour might turn out more modest than expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant, but it means someone dictating a letter aloud. 'Humbler' is not a comparative of humble; it is a person who humbles.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's conduct is their outward behaviour and bearing, which is what this word describes.

clue.text: Back lumps? The last thing a camel needs!

definitions.text: The last thing a camel needs!

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in the opposite order

blocks.note: warts are small lumps on the skin

explanation.surface: A camel already has humps on its back; more lumps are the last thing it wants.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the proverb about the last straw that broke the camel's back, the final small burden that becomes too much.
explanation.definitionFit: In the saying, one final piece of dried stalk added to an overloaded camel snaps its spine.

clue.text: Fool modern IT, within bounds

indicators.note: to bound something is to enclose it, so the words before hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Someone is told to fool around with modern information technology, but within limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Within bounds' reads as a single phrase meaning moderately; split it, and 'within' is part of the string while 'bounds' is the verb enclosing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitwit is a silly or stupid person, which is the noun sense of a fool.

clue.text: Late qualifier in race finally drawn

blocks.note: the late so-and-so is someone who has died
a heat is a qualifying round in a race or competition

explanation.surface: A runner who scraped through a qualifying round is last to finish in the final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like slow to arrive, but it means deceased. The definition overlaps the wordplay: 'race' does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: When two competitors cross the line together, the contest ends in a tie, which is exactly this result.

clue.text: Sad ode composed about a bandit

indicators.note: composing something means putting it together, so these letters are arranged anew
about means around, so one set of letters goes round another

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
as in 'ten pounds a head', a can mean per

explanation.surface: A melancholy poem is written about an outlaw.
explanation.walkthrough: The small word 'a' does real work: in 'twice a day' it means per.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless outlaw of the Wild West kind, so a robber or bandit.

clue.text: Member of school got nurse in trouble

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A pupil got the school nurse into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' suggests pupils, but it is a school of fish, a shoal.
explanation.definitionFit: Fish swimming together form a school, so a large caviar-producing fish can be one member of it.

clue.text: Men’s clothing department displays these

blocks.note: surface reading: a shop floor for menswear shows off its stock
setter's reading: what men wear is simply the definition, and a clothing department is where such items hang

explanation.walkthrough: There is no hidden mechanism to find: the clue is a plain, almost circular description of items of clothing on display in a store.
explanation.definitionFit: Items of clothing such as shirts and coats are what a menswear section of a shop puts out for sale.

clue.text: Root drink, say, a maiden knocked back

indicators.note: knocked back means pushed backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: rum is an alcoholic drink
e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
taken as written
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A young woman downs a drink, perhaps root beer, in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests drinking, which the surface exploits; it actually reverses the letters after the drink. 'Root' is a verb, to search.
explanation.definitionFit: To root about is to search untidily through things, which is the verb sense of rummaging.

clue.text: With no place to go, a gin looks awfully inviting

indicators.note: with no means lacking something, so a chunk is taken away from a word
something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out in a garbled order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a loo is a toilet, the place you go when you need to go

explanation.surface: For someone with nowhere to go, a glass of gin looks very tempting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place to go' looks like a destination, but it is the British slang for a toilet, removed from the middle word before the rest is mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Inviting someone is requesting their company, so the present participle of the verb to request works as a synonym.

clue.text: State often angry about those on vacation

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other
a place on vacation has been vacated, so its insides are gone and only the edge letters remain

blocks.note: irate means angry
first and last letters of this word

explanation.surface: Someone is frequently cross about tourists who are away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Often' seems to describe the anger, but it belongs with 'State' as the definition. 'On vacation' sounds like a holiday, but means emptied out.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to say or perform something again and again, so it means to repeat a statement many times.

clue.text: Pitches left covered in spots

indicators.note: something covered in another thing is wrapped inside it

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
to spot something is to see it, so spots means spies

explanation.surface: Football pitches abandoned for a while are covered with patches of mud or weeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitches' looks like sports grounds and 'spots' like marks; both are other senses, a sales talk and a verb meaning sees.
explanation.definitionFit: A salesperson's pitch is a persuasive patter, which is a long glib speech in the same sense.

clue.text: Receive grant

blocks.note: first meaning: to let someone in, as a hospital takes in a patient
second meaning: to concede a point, as in 'I grant you that'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Receive grant' reads like getting funding; split it into two verbs, each with its own meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both letting a visitor enter a place and conceding that something is true.

clue.text: President that was the beginning of the end

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: first letter of this word
the rump is the rear end of an animal

explanation.surface: A historian says a certain president marked the start of a decline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The beginning of the end' is a stock phrase, but here it is read word by word: the opening letter, then a word for a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Donald Trump served as US president, so his surname is an example of a head of state.

clue.text: Mean about donation

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
a present is a gift

explanation.surface: Someone is being stingy over a charitable gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like the adjective for stingy; it is the verb, to signify.
explanation.definitionFit: When a symbol stands for something it signifies it, which is what both verbs express.

clue.text: Rank rubbish safe to be put outside

indicators.note: a thing put outside another stands round it, wrapping it

blocks.note: sure means safe, as in a sure bet
tat is cheap, worthless stuff

explanation.surface: Stinking garbage is safe to leave out on the street for collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' looks like an adjective for foul-smelling rubbish, but it is the noun, standing; the clue gives the outer word after the inner one.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's standing or reputation in a field is their importance or level, the noun sense of rank.

clue.text: Cheese rind taken from ramen dish in Japan

indicators.note: taking the rind off removes the outer skin, so the edge letters go and the middle stays

blocks.note: Edam is a Dutch cheese
this word with its first and last letters peeled away

explanation.surface: Cheese rind has been removed from a bowl of noodle soup served in Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ramen dish in Japan' runs together naturally, but the definition starts at 'dish'.
explanation.definitionFit: These boiled young soybeans in their pods are a familiar Japanese appetiser or side order.

clue.text: River crossing a forest in two ways: one’s to the east

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so a word is held within others
east is to the right on a map, so in an across entry this goes on the right-hand end

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way; two of them
Epping Forest is an ancient woodland on the edge of London
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A river runs through a forest in two directions, one of them eastward.
explanation.walkthrough: The forest is Epping Forest, north-east of London; it sits between the two street abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of flat rocks placed across a stream lets walkers get over without wading, so they form a crossing.
